podcast.title: Chrysler Job (1996, Brampton)
podcast.body: Aaron worked on the assembly line at a Chrysler plant in Brampton in 1996. It was described as a good-paying job with benefits. "You were working on the line. Working on the line. Yeah. In Brampton. Great job. Good pay."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Billy Talent In Their Own Words: Part 1

podcast.title: MS Awareness Advocacy (2006 onwards)
podcast.body: In 2006, after learning about children as young as three being diagnosed with MS, Aaron decided to publicly share his diagnosis to raise awareness. He actively works with the MS Society of Canada and is involved with FUMS, an organization that hosts benefit concerts and golf tournaments to support MS charities. "he thought it was maybe time that he did what he could to raise awareness of MS."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Stepping Back from Recording Drums (2016)
podcast.body: On January 15, 2016, Aaron Solowoniuk announced via YouTube that he would temporarily step away from recording drums for Billy Talent's upcoming album due to an MS relapse. He explained that his symptoms were slowing him down, and he needed to focus on his health, expressing uncertainty about the duration of his recovery. "I'm not going to be able to play drums on this record. I just need to focus on my health while the record is being recorded."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Band Banker
podcast.body: Aaron Solowaniak was considered the band's "banker" because he used his well-paying job at Chrysler to max out his credit card and fund the band's early demos and studio time when no one else had the means to do so. "We're in hell of a paycheck, though, because he paid for all of our demos. Yeah. Is that true? Yeah. I just, when we were making the demos, I would just max out the credit card to pay for the studio time. And then we'd eventually pay it back. But we just needed money. So, and I had a credit card because I had a job at Chrysler."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Billy Talent In Their Own Words: Part 1

podcast.title: Career vs. Health Benefits Dilemma (Early 2000s)
podcast.body: As Billy Talent gained traction, Aaron faced a choice between continuing his factory job at Chrysler, which offered good benefits covering his expensive MS drugs, and pursuing music with the band, which typically lacked such benefits. He ultimately chose the band, initially keeping his condition a secret. "Working at the Chrysler plant meant good benefits, benefits that covered the cost of the expensive drugs he needed. Meanwhile, rock bands tend not to have any benefits."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Chrysler Job Description
podcast.body: Aaron's job at Chrysler involved inserting six screws every 46 seconds, 500 times a day, at the bottom of a car door using a torque wrench and a sticker. He described it as a "craziest job" where one "leave[s] your brain at the door" and acts "basically a robot." "Oh, man, I would insert six screws every 46 seconds for 500 times a day at the bottom of a door that came up. It was just, it was the craziest job I've ever done in my life because you just leave your brain at the door and you don't really talk to anyone. Sometimes you make friends with people. But for the most part, you're basically a robot."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Billy Talent In Their Own Words: Part 1

podcast.title: Current Health Management Strategy
podcast.body: Aaron Solowoniuk has discontinued all MS medication for three months prior to the interview, opting instead for a routine focused on healthy eating, exercise, and maintaining a positive mindset, as previous newer drugs made him feel worse. He plans to explore other therapies if his current approach proves insufficient. "Right now I've stopped taking all of my drug. I'm three months into no drugs at all. I'm going the eating healthy and exercising route to see how that works because the drugs that I've been taking, the newer ones, haven't really worked for me."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Decision to Not Play on Latest Album
podcast.body: Aaron made the difficult decision not to participate in recording Billy Talent's latest album approximately one month before they were scheduled to enter the studio, after 12 or 13 songs had already been written. At this point, he was using a cane and felt he was pushing himself too hard, acknowledging that his MS was finally slowing him down despite his long-held determination not to let it. "We had written 12 up 13 songs and we were one month away from going into the studio and I just said I can't do it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early MS Diagnosis and Symptoms
podcast.body: Aaron Solowoniuk was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis in 1998 at the age of 24. His initial symptoms included a buzzing sensation in his legs from the hips down, which made walking difficult, and optic neuritis in his left eye, causing significant vision loss, alongside general confusion. "Buzzing legs from my hips down. I could barely walk to my job at Chrysler. I had an optic arthritis in my left eye, so I lost a lot of vision in my eye."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Goal for Return to Drumming
podcast.body: Despite the challenges, Aaron Solowoniuk's ultimate goal is to return to playing drums, leveraging the knowledge gained from listening to his body to come back even stronger. He remains optimistic about his recovery and eventual return to the band. "I'm in rest assured that I am going to do everything I can to get back on the drums. But right now I need to step away for a bit and focus on my health."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Golden Griddle Busboy
podcast.body: Aaron Solowaniak and Ian D'Sa both worked together as busboys at a Golden Griddle restaurant "way, way back in the day." "We both worked at Golden Griddle as busboys together way, way back in the day."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Billy Talent In Their Own Words: Part 1

podcast.title: Long-Term MS Management and Relapse
podcast.body: For over a decade, Aaron managed his MS effectively through a regimen of drugs, prescription adjustments, and a positive outlook, including needle therapy. However, the treatment eventually ceased being effective, leading to a relapse in the six to seven months preceding January 2016, with symptoms causing him to slow down. "I was on this needle therapy for about over a decade. It all seemed to work and then it just stopped. So, feel myself getting slower as I get older, as we all do."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: MS Diagnosis and Career Shift
podcast.body: Aaron was diagnosed with MS, which posed a significant challenge. At 24, he faced the difficult decision of leaving a stable, well-paying job with benefits at Chrysler to pursue his dream of being a drummer, a choice heavily influenced by his personal struggles at the time. This decision marked a "huge rebirth" for both him and the band. "Well, Aaron had been diagnosed with MS, which obviously threw us all in for a loop. ... And for me, at that time, in my life, I had to make the decision of staying at the good job that paid well and had benefits. ... But I was really just chasing this dream of being a drummer. And it just meant so much more to me because I was going through so much hard stuff in my life at that point. So, yeah, it was a huge rebirth for me personally and the band."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Billy Talent In Their Own Words: Part 1

podcast.title: Multiple Sclerosis Diagnosis (Late 1990s)
podcast.body: In the late 1990s, while working on an assembly line at the Chrysler factory in Brampton, Aaron Solowoniuk began experiencing tingling and weakness. He was later diagnosed with multiple sclerosis (MS), an inflammatory disease affecting the nerves. "When he had it checked out, he was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis, an inflammatory disease that messes with the nerves."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Ongoing MS Treatment
podcast.body: Aaron's MS is managed with three weekly injections of an expensive drug, and he is committed to supporting MS charities until a cure is found. "Aaron's own health is under control thanks to three weekly injections of a hideously expensive drug."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Replaced Ben as Drummer
podcast.body: Aaron Solowaniak replaced Ben Kowalewicz as the drummer in the band To Each His Own, impressing the other members with his superior drumming skills. "And it was Aaron. And so I got the boot out of the band."

xref.title: Aaron Solowoniuk's MS Relapse and Album Absence (2016)
xref.body: On January 15, 2016, Aaron announced on YouTube that he was experiencing an MS relapse, which had been slowing him down for six to seven months. The symptoms made it difficult to perform daily tasks and play drums. He decided to step away from recording drums for the "Afraid of Heights" album to focus on his health, as he was unsure how long his recovery would take. The band fully supported his decision and brought in Jordan Hastings as a fill-in drummer.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Band Support for Aaron Solowoniuk and FUMS (2016)
xref.body: Billy Talent, their management, and their record label (Warner Music Canada) are 100% supportive of Aaron in his struggle with MS. They established a charity called FUMS (Fuck U MS) to raise money for MS research. At a music festival on May 29, 2016, a band member (Ben Kowalewicz) addressed the crowd, expressing the band's love, care, and commitment to Aaron, and thanking Jordan Hastings for filling in. The speaker referred to Aaron as "Mr. A. S. Lua," which appears to be a mis-transcription of his full name, Aaron Solowoniuk.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Relapse and Stepping Back from Recording (January 15, 2016)
xref.body: In a YouTube message posted on January 15, 2016, Aaron Solowoniuk announced he was experiencing an MS relapse that had slowed him down over the past 6-7 months, making even simple tasks like climbing stairs daunting and drumming very tiring. Due to his health, he decided he couldn't play drums on the band's upcoming record and needed to focus on getting healthy. "On January 15th, 2016, Aaron posted a message on YouTube. Just wanted to let everybody know what is going on in Billy Talent World right now. The album is being recorded as we speak... Over the past six or seven months. I've been dealing with a relapse."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Aaron Solowoniuk's Treatment and Recovery
xref.body: After his relapse, Aaron decided to stop taking his MS medication for three months and explore alternative therapies, focusing on healthy eating and exercise. He expressed a goal to come back stronger, listening to his body more carefully, after having previously pushed himself too hard, to the point of walking with a cane. In 2017, he made a return to the stage, playing one song in Poland, his first performance in a year.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Band Support and Charitable Work
xref.body: Despite Aaron Solowoniuk's ongoing health challenges and reduced ability to play, Billy Talent continues to support him. The band also engages in numerous charitable initiatives with MS groups, demonstrating their commitment to raising awareness and funds for the disease. "It's been tough for Aaron and he hasn't been able to play with the band as much as he'd hoped but he's still with the guys and the guys are still supporting him, including with numerous charitable initiatives with MS groups."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Exploring Alternative MS Management
xref.body: Aaron Solowoniuk decided to stop taking all prescribed drugs for three months, as newer medications had not worked and made him feel worse. He is now pursuing a regimen of healthy eating and exercise, hoping to manage his MS symptoms naturally, with a plan to explore newer therapies if this approach proves ineffective. "Right now I've stopped taking all of my... I'm three months into no drugs at all. I'm going the eating healthy and exercising route to see how that works because the drugs that I've been taking, the newer ones, haven't really worked for me and they kind of made me feel worse."

He was highly praised for his skill and contribution. His first two shows with Billy Talent were in Russia, and his third was at the Rock am Ring Festival in Germany.
